cards.lore: From 400 AD to the 14th century, surviving religious music was entirely monophonic vocal chant. Common-practice tonality didn't exist yet.
cards.power: Limit your opponent to playing one single melodic line card per turn.

cards.lore: The most notable style of the Middle Ages; highly effective for pacifying crowds before polyphony ruined everything.
cards.power: Hypnotize the arena, rendering all high-flying moves useless for two turns.

cards.lore: Thomas Tallis defined the Renaissance era with vocal music so densely polyphonic that clergymen found it impossibly chaotic to relate to.
cards.power: Overbook the ring with 40 active wrestlers, causing massive confusion damage.

cards.lore: Wealthy patrons funded secular chansons and madrigals, aggressively blurring the lines between religious and secular music.
cards.power: Buy off the referee and fund a secular madrigal distraction.

cards.lore: The stereotypical keyboard instrument of the Baroque era, weaponized by the elite before the piano replaced it.
cards.power: Pluck your opponent's nerves; this weapon's terraced dynamics cannot be silenced once deployed.

cards.lore: The Classical era developed this dominant structure: create a theme, develop it in the middle, and lazily restate it at the end.
cards.power: Force your opponent to repeat their opening move at the exact end of the match.

cards.lore: A compositional form where a solo instrument alternates passages with a full orchestra, popularized by spotlight-hungry performers.
cards.power: Tag in a solo instrument to dominate the larger orchestra for massive damage.

cards.lore: Codified in the Baroque era; Classical and Romantic composers used it almost nothing else, ensuring maximum predictable drudgery.
cards.power: Nullify all weird time signature cards; forcefully reset the match rhythm to an insufferably simple 4/4.

cards.lore: Popularized in the Romantic era to push instruments to their limits with lusher, denser sounds and unrelenting sustain.
cards.power: Hold your submission lock indefinitely without ever losing stamina.

cards.lore: The Second Viennese School discarded common practice tonality entirely for continuous transformations of twelve-tone series.
cards.power: Disorient opponent by removing the musical key entirely; attacks cannot be blocked.

cards.lore: Modernist composers demanded instruments be used in unusual, rule-breaking ways to generate terrifying new timbres.
cards.power: Use a traditional instrument as a blunt percussion weapon.

cards.lore: Post-WWII composers like Stockhausen and Boulez pushed the serialism of Schoenberg to its absolute mathematical, unlistenable extreme.
cards.power: Lecture the crowd until they boo, converting their heat into sheer elitist power.

cards.lore: Haydn wrote so many good quartets (two violins, viola, cello) that later composers felt aggressively pressured to prove themselves in the exact same format.
cards.power: Execute an inescapable, highly respected 4-on-1 team assault.

cards.lore: An ensemble built from two trumpets, a horn, a trombone, and a tuba to maximize sheer sonic impact.
cards.power: Blow out the opponent's eardrums with overwhelming metallic volume.

cards.lore: A tightly-knit assault unit consisting of a violin, a cello, and a piano, demanding equal technical chops from all three members.
cards.power: Strike simultaneously with bowed string precision and percussive keyboard weight.

cards.lore: A quintet formed by adding a horn to a flute, oboe, clarinet, and bassoon for maximum tonal variety and deception.
cards.power: Choke your opponent out with reeds and superior breath control.

cards.lore: Large groups pushed to their limits; but remember the ultimate misconception: not all orchestral music is classical music!
cards.power: Summon every string, brass, woodwind, and percussion card in your deck simultaneously.

cards.lore: A massive grouping of vocalists utilized to elevate the perceived divine importance and emotional weight of a piece.
cards.power: Drop a heavenly vocal harmony from the rafters to completely distract the opponent.

cards.lore: A beloved trope where the maestro physically battles the orchestra, using sheer kinetic fury to force them into compliance.
cards.power: Dictate the match pace with frantic baton swings; ignore all established rules.

cards.lore: The ultimate tension-building tool in the composer's arsenal, ensuring the audience knows a massive hit is coming.
cards.power: Interrupt any opponent's promo with a deafening percussion strike.

cards.lore: The undisputed master of the Baroque era, famous for dense religious polyphony and mathematically merciless fugues.
cards.power: Lock your opponent in a relentless, inescapable counterpoint hold.

cards.lore: The father of the symphony and string quartet; he built the structural rules that everyone else was forced to follow.
cards.power: Dictate the match format; your opponent is forced to fight strictly in Sonata Form.

cards.lore: The composer behind the 'Hallelujah Chorus,' who leveraged the patron model to achieve undeniable rock-star status.
cards.power: Summon a massive chorus to prematurely declare your inevitable victory.

cards.lore: The most famous piece in D minor — which modern musicologists now believe Bach didn't actually compose at all.
cards.power: Steal an opponent's signature move and successfully claim you invented it.

cards.lore: The defining genius of the Classical Era, pushing homophony and independent secular music to an absolute peak.
cards.power: Humiliate your opponent by perfectly countering their finishing move without looking.

cards.lore: The pioneer of the Romantic era; his later works, like the Fifth Symphony, forever shattered classical constraints.
cards.power: Ignore opponent's trash talk entirely; attack with pure, unblockable Romantic fury.

cards.lore: A Romantic-era master who pushed the limits of solo piano technique with blisteringly fast pieces like the 'Revolutionary' Etude.
cards.power: Dazzle the crowd with a lightning-fast flurry of solo piano strikes.

cards.lore: A common trope where compositions, especially concertos, call for some pretty mad, highly gratuitous performing chops.
cards.power: Waste an entire turn doing something incredibly difficult just to flex on the crowd.

cards.lore: Set the standard for epic film music today; he pioneered the Leitmotif to permanently brand his mythological characters into your brain.
cards.power: Extend the match to 15 hours; your opponent quits out of sheer exhaustion.

cards.lore: A programmatic Romantic composer who legitimately thought classical music should feature literal cannons in chromatic concert halls.
cards.power: Fire actual live artillery into the ring; obliterating area-of-effect damage.

cards.lore: A 19th-century virtuoso performer who was legitimately treated like a pop star by the swelling European middle classes.
cards.power: Incite a riot in the crowd; opponent is trampled by adoring swooning elites.

cards.lore: A trope where the orchestra hits its absolute emotional peak; carefully timed to underscore a violently dramatic moment.
cards.power: Drop the entire brass and percussion section on the opponent's head simultaneously.

cards.lore: Shattered social contract; his ballets so jarringly polyrhythmic that audiences literally rioted at the premiere.
cards.power: Play 'The Rite of Spring'; the furious audience attacks your opponent for you.

cards.lore: A 20th-century experimentalist who pushed the definition of musical understanding to its absolute breaking point.
cards.power: Do absolutely nothing for 4 minutes and 33 seconds; opponent takes massive psychological damage.

cards.lore: Blurred the boundaries entirely, proving that classical and popular styles can co-exist in amazing, highly profitable ways.
cards.power: Tag in a jazz musician to perform a highly illegal cross-genre strike.

cards.lore: Johann Pachelbel accidentally invented the most overused, copied chord progression in the history of Western wedding music.
cards.power: Recycle your last three moves infinitely without spending any energy.

cards.lore: Performance instructions are marked in Italian, analytical terms in German. The genre inherently demands gratuitous foreign language.
cards.power: Scream performance instructions in Italian until the referee cannot understand your opponent.

cards.lore: Indicated with a simple pause in the score, expecting the performer to improvise their way to glory.
cards.power: Pause the match to improvise up a solo so impressive, completely unblockable.

cards.lore: A recurring musical phrase associated with a particular person, place, or idea, heavily installed into our brains by Wagner.
cards.power: Play your signature theme song; your opponent will break before you even enter the ring.

cards.lore: Complex rhythms allowed classical music to develop beyond the basic, predictable brevity of pop song structures.
cards.power: Attack in 13/16 time; your opponent physically cannot time their counter.

cards.lore: Used to instantly signify impending doom, courtesy of compositions set to Latin by Verdi, Dvorak, and Mozart.
cards.power: Summon the wrath of a Requiem Mass to instantly drop the temperature in the arena.

cards.lore: The ultimate instrument of gothic intimidation, ensuring everyone in the room knows the heel has officially arrived.
cards.power: Trap your opponent in a gothic cathedral and inflict continuous sonic dread.

cards.lore: When snobs and aristocrats attend a classical performance solely because it makes them look 'cultured' to their peers.
cards.power: Fill the front row with cultured elites; their polite applause heals your damage.

cards.lore: The ultimate shorthand in soundtracks: if someone is singing Italian vibrato, something incredibly tragic is happening.
cards.power: Underscore the match with a tragic aria; your opponent weeps uncontrollably.

cards.lore: A myth perpetuated because classical concerts demand intense, silent listening rather than rowdy rock-show behavior.
cards.power: Put the audience to sleep so the referee doesn't see your illegal chair shot.

cards.lore: The deeply ingrained pretension that centuries-old music is inherently superior to anything recently composed.
cards.power: Immune to all modern attacks (new); nothing composed before 1820 can hurt you.

cards.lore: Since the music is well over 100 years old, copyright expired, making it a free buffet for cheap media producers.
cards.power: Steal your opponent's theme music without paying them any royalties.

cards.lore: Painstakingly restoring ancient instruments and demanding composers wear Gorgeous Period Dress to achieve 'authenticity.'
cards.power: Force opponent to fight using painful, un-upgraded medieval equipment.

cards.lore: Classical music requires a broad dynamic range, from solo flutes to full orchestra, ruining the pop-industry's compression tactics.
cards.power: Refuse to compress your audio; your sudden dynamic spikes deal critical unblockable damage.

cards.cardName: Rock is Authentic, Pop is Shallow
cards.lore: The endless industry argument, completely ignoring that heavily classically-trained musicians play in all styles.
cards.power: Pit two rival factions against each other while you sneak a pinfall attempt on the enemy with supreme superiority.

cards.lore: When classical themes blatantly show up in music from other genres, proving classical was just the pop of the past.
cards.power: Cash in your classical credibility for a massive mainstream pop-chart buff.

cards.lore: Heavy metal bands frequently incorporate classical scales, harmonies, and entire orchestras into their brutal sonic assaults.
cards.power: Equip your electric guitar with a 60-piece orchestra backing track.

cards.lore: A tremendous number of Classical works lack creative titles, using a simple statement of genre, number, and key.
cards.power: Confuse the opponent to death by naming your Finisher 'Symphony No. 9 in D Minor, Op. 125.'

cards.lore: 'Classical' music refers to the tradition of music being written down, up until the invention of recording technology changed everything.
cards.power: Trap your opponent's performance on a wax cylinder, replaying their defeat forever.

cards.lore: Classical music is alive and kicking; modern film composers like John Williams are romantic to their very bones.
cards.power: Prove the genre isn't dead by attacking with a living, breathing cinematic film score.

cards.lore: The Kayfabe is real. The music is BIZZARO. The Kanon is KAYFAB. Stay fluffy, marks!
cards.power: Tear up the rulebook, pour watercolors on the ring, and declare yourself the winner.
